other-interests-320afcc118.headline: AI refutes 30-year-old mathematical assumption in computer science
other-interests-320afcc118.fulltext:
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, claims its AI models have disproven the exponential time hypothesis – a fundamental assumption that underpins computer science.
“This came as a complete surprise, a shock,” says Fedor Fomin at the University of Bergen in Norway. “Nobody I know expected it.”
Proposed nearly 30 years ago, the exponential time hypothesis (ETH) tries to put a limit on how quickly computers can solve certain logical puzzles.
Advertisement
The simplest way would be to try every possible combination of true or false for each part of the puzzle. ETH proposes that, although it may be possible to do this quicker with shortcuts, the amount of work needed has to grow exponentially as the puzzle gets bigger.
OpenAI, however, says its models have devised an algorithm that can beat the previously assumed speed limit for solving logical puzzles, apparently proving ETH false. “Assuming that it is confirmed, this is an enormous breakthrough,” says Leslie Goldberg at the University of Oxford.
Many computer science findings assume ETH is true. If it isn’t, the conclusions they establish about computational limits become useless. “It would require a complete revision of several areas of algorithms and complexity,” says Fomin, who says a textbook he wrote on the subject would become obsolete if the finding holds.
ETH is linked to a long-standing maths problem known as P versus NP, which concerns whether a problem whose answer is easy to check is also easy to solve. If ETH were true, it would have implied that the answer was no. But disproving ETH wouldn’t mean the answer is yes. “This doesn’t have a direct impact on P versus NP, so we should not view it as progress towards P versus NP,” says Goldberg.
The result was announced alongside other breakthroughs in maths and physics in a blog post on 26 October.
In mathematics, OpenAI says its AI has proved a 1991 conjecture that waves cannot remain intensely focused for long. If confirmed, this would also answer enduring questions about how thin a shape can be while also containing line segments that point in every direction, as well as how waves spread.
In theoretical physics, OpenAI claims to have proven that quantum field theories – including quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong force holding quarks together – make sense mathematically, rather than just producing predictions that match experiments. The findings also touch on the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory, part of a million-dollar mathematical problem, but don’t resolve the entire challenge. That work hasn’t been released publicly while an external group led by Nobel laureate David Gross examines it.
OpenAI says it verified the ETH result using Lean, a piece of software that checks mathematical proofs. Stefan Szeider at TU Wien in Austria has looked at what OpenAI has released and says he expects it to withstand scrutiny, although he says researchers still need to check that the formally proven statement means what its authors say it means.
To do so, OpenAI has commissioned an independent group, including Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, both at the University of California, San Diego, who helped propose ETH, to examine the findings. In an open letter, the group says it could “change an important part of theoretical computer science”.
The speed at which AI is solving maths problems and the way AI firms are releasing their findings have concerned some academics. Magnus Wahlström at Royal Holloway, University of London, describes the phenomenon as “mathematics done by press”, worrying that proprietary models can suddenly overturn months of researchers’ work.
Bart Jansen at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands describes OpenAI’s work on ETH as “ingenious”, “spectacular” and “awe-inspiring – but also humbling.” “It really makes you think about the future of mathematics, algorithms and academia,” he says.
Clément Canonne at the University of Sydney says proving something and understanding why it is true aren’t the same thing. “The web collapsed, and we looked behind,” he says of the network of findings relying on ETH. “We have no idea why yet.”
OpenAI says it is experimenting with an approach in which independent academics organise efforts to verify and explain the results. But Fomin welcomes the disruption. “This result destroys a lot, but it also opens many new opportunities and new questions that nobody expected,” he says. “One shouldn’t complain about having too many interesting mathematical breakthroughs to try to digest,” says Wahlström.

ai-2d27ef900c.headline: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban
ai-2d27ef900c.fulltext:
AI bots flooded a government consultation with tens of thousands of fake responses in a failed attempt to stop the UK’s ban on disposable vapes.
Three-quarters of all the responses to the 2023 consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, in what is thought to be the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.
The attempt to manipulate the outcome of the consultation was disclosed on Tuesday in research published in the journal Tobacco Control by the health policy experts Dr Nason Maani, from the University of Edinburgh, and Prof Anna Gilmore, of the University of Bath.
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) used bot-detection methods to identify that 90,835 of the 118,756 responses it received, 76%, were submitted by bots.
All but two of those 90,835 automated responses answered the same question in the “smoke free generation” consultation, in which they opposed Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government’s plan to ban disposable vapes. The submissions were “often duplicated many times and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses”, the DHSC said.
The bombardment “appears to be the first documented instance of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation”, the researchers said.
Maani added that while this attempt was identified, “the threat is that future campaigns become harder to catch, and what we can’t catch, we don’t know about. Such campaigns are a threat because they raise the possibility of a handful of powerful interests looking like a mass movement.”
The DHSC excluded the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. Keir Starmer’s Labour government inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes.
Caroline Cerny, the deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “Evidence that AI bots have been used to swamp a Department of Health consultation is deeply concerning.
“Given the tobacco industry’s history of seeking to undermine public health regulation, we need to be alert to the risk that technological advances can be used to further commercial interests around health policy and put safeguards in place.
“Decisions that affect public health must be based on sound evidence and expertise, not manipulated response numbers.”
Azzurra Moores, the associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, described the attempt to derail the ban as “pretty alarming”.
“Public consultations are one of the main ways government opens up its decision-making, so any interference with them is a serious concern,” she said. “These findings are pretty alarming: if a consultation can be swamped like this, it stops telling policymakers what the public actually thinks and undermines trust in the process.
“This is a problem without easy answers. Every barrier that keeps bots out also makes it harder for real people to take part, and AI makes fake responses far harder to spot. Interference can adapt faster than departments can update their checks. Better screening and more transparency will help, but there’s no single fix.”
The DHSC said its “robust controls” identified the attempt to influence the consultation.
A spokesperson said: “We always have robust controls in place to prevent the manipulation of our public consultations, and those controls worked effectively in this case.
“As a result, the fake responses were removed, and the consultation helped inform the landmark action we are taking to create a smoke-free generation.
“We will remain alert to interference of this kind in future consultation processes, and we will not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.”

ai-b007bafd9f.headline: Nvidia backs Indian startup helping companies run AI models with fewer GPUs
ai-b007bafd9f.fulltext:
As the AI boom strains computing capacity, Nvidia has backed Indian startup Simplismart in a $14 million funding round, betting on software that helps companies run AI models more efficiently and, in some cases, with fewer GPUs.
Nvidia participated in the all-primary Series B round alongside Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax, with Dallas Venture Capital leading the investment. The deal values the four-year-old startup at about $100 million, including the new funding.
Companies are nowadays spending heavily on GPUs to power AI applications, but running those models reliably and economically at scale remains a challenge. Different workloads demand distinct trade-offs between speed, cost, and performance. Deploying and operating AI models to meet business requirements often also requires complex adjustments. Simplismart says its software automates much of that work, tailoring how models run on existing computing infrastructure instead of requiring customers to manage those configurations themselves.
“Nobody actually needs the fastest or the cheapest inference,” Amritanshu Jain (pictured above, left), co-founder and CEO of Simplismart, said in an interview. He added that companies instead need to run AI models at speeds and costs that make sense for their specific applications.
Simplismart’s software sits between AI models and the computing infrastructure they run on and adjusts how models are deployed and managed to meet customers’ requirements. It says it can optimize factors such as how quickly a model responds, how many requests it handles, and how much computing power it consumes, helping companies get more out of their existing GPU stack.
The Bengaluru-based startup offers companies a way to deploy and run AI models through its own platform or within their existing cloud and on-premises infrastructure. It also provides tools to fine-tune models, automatically scale computing resources as demand changes, and monitor performance. Additionally, Simplismart allows cloud providers to build and operate their own AI inference services on GPU infrastructure using its software.
Simplismart says it helped AI video-generation platform InVideo cut its GPU serving costs by 56% using its software. The startup also works with AI video companies HeyGen and Higgsfield, as well as enterprise AI startup Ema, among others. Moreover, Indian cloud provider Yotta uses Simplismart’s technology to power the serverless AI inference service within its Shakti Studio platform.
Simplismart’s annualized revenue run rate has grown 14-fold over the past six months to an eight-figure sum, Jain told TechCrunch. The figure is based on recent customer usage rather than contracted recurring revenue and excludes revenue passed through to infrastructure providers, the company said. He did not disclose the exact figure.
More than half of Simplismart’s revenue comes from the U.S., despite the startup having more customers in India, Jain said.
Alongside its investment, Nvidia has been working with Simplismart on technical integrations, including around its Dynamo inference software, Jain told TechCrunch. The collaboration involves Simplismart’s engineers and Nvidia’s solutions architects, while Nvidia has also helped introduce the startup to potential customers and partners, Jain stated.
Interestingly, the investment presents an apparent paradox as Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI chips, is backing software that can help companies run some workloads with fewer GPUs. Jain, however, argued that making AI inference more efficient could ultimately benefit Nvidia by making its hardware more attractive to customers and encouraging wider adoption of AI applications.
Simplismart is serving customers in an increasingly crowded market for AI inference software, competing with offerings from Nvidia itself, as well as major cloud providers and hyperscalers including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. A growing number of startups are also developing tools to make AI models faster and cheaper to run as there is growing demand in this segment, driven by rising demand for AI applications and the need to make better use of expensive GPU resources.
“Where we tend to win is where people have to be more stringent on their SLAs [service-level agreements] and TCO [total cost of ownership],” Jain said, referring to demanding performance requirements and tight cost constraints. Unlike rivals that offer preset options for faster or cheaper inference, Simplismart aims to find a balance tailored to each customer’s needs, he said.
Founded in 2022 by former Oracle engineer Jain and former Google engineer Devansh Ghatak (pictured above, right), Simplismart grew out of the pair’s experience building and deploying machine-learning systems. The two met while studying at BITS Pilani, and the startup now employs 58 people, Jain said.
Simplismart plans to use the new funding to expand its presence in the U.S., grow its team, and invest further in developing its inference software. Jain told TechCrunch that the U.S. remains a key market for the startup as it looks to build on its existing customer base there.
The funding announcement follows a report by Indian English daily The Economic Times that Simplismart was in talks to raise $40 million to $50 million at a valuation of $300 million to $400 million. Asked about the report, Jain declined to comment, saying the startup was not actively fundraising. He added that the Series B was closed and would not be extended.

Key Takeaways
- Innodata stock fell 28% after reports that it abruptly laid off nearly 550 employees in India, with more cuts in the Philippines.
- The termination notices reportedly pointed to a "ramp-down of the business assignment," which raises the question of whether customer work is shrinking.
- Innodata's two largest customers made up 71% of second-quarter revenue, so one lost program could put the 2027 growth estimate at risk.
- Innodata hasn't commented. Its third-quarter report on Nov. 5 is the first real chance to hear from management.
Innodata (INOD:NASDAQ) stock sank 28% today after reports that the AI data company abruptly laid off nearly 550 employees in India on Monday, with more cuts in the Philippines.
Innodata hasn't said anything yet. But how the cuts reportedly happened, and the reason given for them, is what has investors running for the exit.
Logged Out Mid-Shift
India Today broke the story Tuesday morning. Employees reportedly started Monday like any other workday, then lost access to company systems partway through it.
One laid-off employee in Delhi told India Today: "One by one, we started losing access to our official devices. Laptops were logged out, and official IDs deactivated."
Termination emails reportedly landed in workers' personal inboxes later that day. They cited a "ramp-down of the business assignment" and said the decision wasn't about individual performance.
That reason is the part shareholders should care about.
Innodata Lives and Dies by Two Customers
Innodata's business leans heavily on a handful of big tech clients. Its two largest made up 71% of second-quarter revenue, according to its 10-Q. The reported ramp-down raises the possibility that customer work is shrinking. It doesn't tell us which customer, how much revenue is at stake, or whether the cut is temporary.
And the Street's growth expectations depend on that work. Analysts expect revenue to jump from $252 million in 2025 to $360 million this year, then $460 million in 2027:
Most of 2026 is already done, so this year's number has less room to slip. If a program is gone, 2027 takes the hit.

agritech-a9f0eefbbc.headline: Weak monsoon, crop failures, force farmers to cut spending | India News
agritech-a9f0eefbbc.fulltext:
Weak monsoon, crop failures, force farmers to cut spending
India’s weakest monsoon in over a decade raises concerns about farm output, winter sowing and rural spending
Farmer Ramesh Valvi, 34, hoped to buy a ₹4.5 lakh tractor for his three-hectare farm in Maharashtra’s Mandvi village. He saved ₹60,000 and hoped to earn another ₹50,000 for the ₹2 lakh down payment. Valvi planned to arrange the remaining amount from his brother, a construction contractor.
The plan is now on hold as Valvi’s maize and tur crops failed after rains stopped. ₹40,000 he invested in his land is also lost. Valvi expects to only break even, leaving little room for the tractor purchase. There is not enough water even to drink, and he sees little chance of sowing a rabi crop in the winter, unless water becomes available.
With no income expected from another harvest, he expects to use his savings to feed his family. His remaining hope is compensation through crop insurance. Valvi’s predicament echoes many as India’s weakest monsoon in more than a decade raises concerns about farm output, winter sowing and rural spending.
The effects are beginning to show in fertiliser and farm machinery sales, while low reservoir levels threaten to extend the damage beyond the monsoon crop.
The weak monsoon
The southwest monsoon, which delivers 70% of Indian rains, started weak. The country registered its fifth-driest June since national statistics began in 1901. There was a 39.8% fall from the long-period average. Rains picked up briefly bringing some relief in July but plunged again in August, recording a 16.3% deficit and the hottest August since 1901 as El Nino conditions strengthened.
The monsoon ended with a 12.6% downfall, the fourth-lowest since 2001. There were also sharp regional variations. East and northeast India received 25% less rainfall than normal. Southern peninsular India had 24% less and northwest India 6% less rain. Key agricultural states also recorded poor rains. Bihar had a deficit of 32%, Punjab 41%, Marathwada 39% and Kerala 28%. Overall, 17 meteorological subdivisions, covering 42% of the country’s area, recorded deficient rainfall during the season.
The decadal weak monsoon has left parts of the country with inadequate soil moisture just as farmers prepare for the rabi season. The weak monsoon has also left reservoir storages down. Despite higher storages recorded at the beginning of the season due to above-average rains last year, reservoir levels depleted to 68.6% of capacity on October 15, against 90.8% a year earlier and against the 10-year average of 82.1%.
According to a Barclays report, over 37% of districts had severe or extreme soil-moisture deficits. Rain-fed areas are particularly vulnerable because they have less access to irrigation. For farmers who have lost their kharif crops, a failure to sow rabi crops could mean another season with little or no farm income.
Fertiliser sales slide
The lack of rain affected not just Valvi’s crop but also how much fertiliser he could apply. He usually applies it four times during the crop cycle, but managed only two rounds this year because there was not enough water. The fertiliser he did apply failed to spread into the soil properly, he said, and pests attacked the crop.
National fertiliser sales have also weakened. Industry estimates suggest sales of complex fertilisers fell by more than 20% in April-September from a year earlier. Urea sales also declined, despite higher domestic production and imports.
Poor rainfall may have discouraged farmers from spending on inputs, though supply constraints and higher raw-material costs have also affected some fertiliser categories. With little water available even for drinking, Valvi does not expect to sow a rabi crop. His savings, which he had set aside to buy a tractor, will now go towards feeding his family. He is hoping for compensation through crop insurance to help him tide over the losses.
Muted tractor demand
India, still being a largely agrarian economy, has a significant percentage of the population dependent on agriculture for a healthy income. Prospects for that have turned sour this year owing to the bad monsoon.
Tractor retail sales fell 12.58% month-on-month to 76,906 units in September, according to the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, but were still 13.75% higher than a year earlier. On a year-on-year basis, sales were down 18%. A Barclays report said the effect of crop losses on tractor purchases could become clearer in early 2027, as lower farm earnings prompt some farmers to delay expensive purchases.
For Valvi, that decision has already been made. With his kharif crop gone and the next sowing uncertain, the money he set aside for a tractor will instead go towards food.

india-91b856760d.headline: What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
india-91b856760d.fulltext:
When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. ai-a878112837.headline: General Compute raises $100 million Series A, countering the neocloud disaster narrative
ai-a878112837.fulltext:
CoreWeave, a publicly traded neocloud that rents out computing power for AI, has seen its stock price fall to a 12-month low, and Elon Musk is flexing $40 billion in debt for buying computing capacity and predicting that “200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.” It’s not exactly the ideal week to announce a Series A for a neocloud.
General Compute co-founder and CEO Finn Puklowski is unfazed. He’s bullish on CoreWeave’s chances, and thinks Musk is just talking his book to drive down the prices of the GPUs he wants to buy. Fears of a chip-led collapse are “massively overstated. I have people calling me up every single week asking me to do TPUs, GPUs, any chip, to get them more compute.”
Just as important, he says, Anthropic’s bullish S-1 is “settling fears for today.”
General Compute has found a niche building its cloud out of specialized inference chips built by Nvidia rivals. The company struck a $400 million deal to purchase new chips from SambaNova — the first debt financing of inference chips — and now has added Positron and Cerebras to its portfolio of chip suppliers.
A deal with a large customer worth $100 million in annual recurring revenue has paved the way for the company to raise $100 million in Series A funding led by Blackbird Ventures and Abstract Ventures. Valued at $60 million after a May seed round, General Compute is now worth $800 million post-money to its investors.
The startup’s strategy is to zig where others zag. It focused on chips built for inference while everyone else chased GPUs. And instead of taking on a complex effort to build huge data centers, it uses smaller power sources, rents space in other companies’ data centers, and converts former bitcoin-mining sites into places that run AI models.
That approach means General Compute isn’t going to catapult into the top ranks of neoclouds or compete with hyperscalers any time soon. But it’s also not subject to the constraints that come with building data centers from scratch. When General Compute has chips, it will have someplace to plug them in. Puklowski expects the company to deploy 75 megawatts of computing capacity in 2027, and he suspects he will have access to 200 megawatts of power — “more than we can probably fund and get hardware for.”
Still, the plan has a limit. Puklowski’s financing work isn’t done — “capital is going to be a full-time job for me, both on debt and equity,” he told TechCrunch.
The startup has found key customers in cloud companies that specialize in offering developers high-speed inference; General Compute provides the bare metal, or raw servers with no software layered on top, for them to bring their offerings to market. James Palmer, a principal at Blackbird who co-led the round, said his firm’s confidence in General Compute comes in part from an investment in Baseten, an inference cloud company.
“We’ve been proximate to their journey over the last 10 months and observing the wild growth story that [Baseten] has gone on, and the demand for open weight inference, and for companies owning their own intelligence,” Palmer told TechCrunch. When it comes to General Compute, he said, “Cerebras, Positron, SambaNova, all need distribution partners who can take them to scale, who can navigate the complexity of the physical world.”
Executives at all three chipmakers sang General Compute’s praises to TechCrunch, each noting the importance of the company’s focus on making the economics of AI cloud compute work. “Everyone in this market is selling speed,” Rodrigo Liang, SambaNova’s CEO and co-founder, said. “The real question is whether you can make money doing it.”

ai-cac2f27240.headline: Former Deepmind researcher thinks AlphaGo's playbook can cure AI hallucinations
ai-cac2f27240.fulltext:
Former Deepmind researcher thinks AlphaGo's playbook can cure AI hallucinations
Key Points
- Former Deepmind researcher Thore Graepel founded Metis Reasoning to make AI systems more reliable and verifiable, using AlphaGo's approach as a blueprint.
- The method separates knowledge from model weights and stores it in an external ledger, where an independent module checks every assumption against evidence.
- The approach aims to cut hallucinations and provide source-backed explanations, but so far it exists only as a theoretical framework with no working system.
Former Deepmind researcher Thore Graepel wants to build AI systems that track what they know and check every conclusion against evidence. Larger language models won't fix this problem, his team says.
Thore Graepel believes the same idea that let AlphaGo beat Go professional Lee Sedol in 2016 can make AI systems more reliable, including in robots. The former Deepmind researcher founded Metis Reasoning and laid out the approach at Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin, where the chipmaker has been expanding its platform for robotics and physical AI with the goal of turning robotics' data problem into a compute problem.
A knowledge ledger instead of knowledge baked into model weights
Today's language models amount to just AlphaGo's prediction network, which suggested possible moves, according to Metis. AlphaGo paired that network with a systematic search through game sequences and found the famous Move 37, a move the network would have given a human player roughly a one-in-ten-thousand chance of making. Metis wants to bring that kind of search to general reasoning.
Doing so requires what the company's paper calls an explicit knowledge ledger, comparable to the game board. Similar ideas already exist: Microsoft's GraphRAG organizes knowledge outside model weights in a knowledge graph, and Google's AlphaGeometry2 pairs a language model with a symbolic engine that verifies mathematical proofs. Metis wants to extend those principles to open questions in the real world.
Its knowledge ledger records what is known, how confident the system is, and which questions remain open. A separate module checks new entries against calculations, formal proofs, or empirical evidence, and when an assumption falls away, every conclusion that depended on it gets re-evaluated. A "move" can be a question, an experiment, or a challenge to an existing assumption; the system picks whichever one reduces uncertainty about the original question the most, ultimately delivering either an answer or a justified abstention.
As in AlphaGo, two neural networks suggest and evaluate moves, trained on logged prior investigations but unable to override the verification rules. Metis says the setup should produce fewer hallucinations, explanations with source citations, and knowledge that can be changed or deleted without retraining. Because reasoning breaks into small steps, the approach could also favor smaller models running on edge devices and in robots.
Companies still don't trust language models enough to deploy them
More data and compute improve language models but don't solve the technology's fundamental problems, according to Metis: the models fabricate answers, their reasoning chains can't be verified, and their knowledge is locked inside the weights. Hallucinations come from the training process itself, the paper argues, because models learn to produce plausible text rather than true text, and even the chains of thought in today's reasoning models often fail to show how an answer was actually reached.
That, the paper says, is why AI has had so little economic impact so far. When an agent acts on behalf of a company, errors are hard to trace back to their source and wrong knowledge can't be removed from the model. AI took off in software engineering because code is easy to test and roll back, but in medicine, finance, chip design, and robotics, the paper argues, AI needs to be verifiable from the ground up.
The white paper describes only a research program, with no working system, no benchmarks, and no comparisons with current reasoning models. The team acknowledges that the real world, unlike Go, provides only partial information, that evidence can be expensive to obtain, and that some questions simply have no answer. The biggest open question is how a verified knowledge ledger would take shape in messy domains beyond textbook examples, given that symbolic AI systems once failed precisely because all their knowledge had to be entered by hand.
After Silver and Rocktäschel, another Deepmind veteran strikes out on his own
Graepel earned his PhD in machine learning in Berlin in 2001, according to his website. At Microsoft Research he helped build TrueSkill, the matchmaking system behind Xbox Live. He then moved to Deepmind, where he worked on AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero. After a stint at Altos Labs he most recently served on Google Deepmind's post-AGI team, which he left over the summer. He also holds the machine learning chair at University College London. According to Bloomberg, Graepel is raising a low tens-of-millions round for Metis, with a follow-on of several hundred million dollars at a higher valuation already in the works.
He's the latest architect of Deepmind's best-known breakthroughs to build something outside Google. Former colleague David Silver founded Ineffable Intelligence and closed the largest seed round of any European startup. Tim Rocktäschel co-founded Recursive, now valued at $4.65 billion. Others are going straight to competitors. According to the Financial Times, Deepmind dissolved the team behind AlphaFold, and Nobel laureate John Jumper left for Anthropic with two colleagues. CNBC traces the talent drain partly to limited internal access to Google's TPU chips and bureaucracy, while Deepmind itself is losing its independence and founder Demis Hassabis has stepped back from day-to-day operations.

indian-startups-6b73d31626.fulltext:
Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with the bulk of investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1.
It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year.
China and the US lead
The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested.
The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics, a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics, which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round.
In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI, which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain.
Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics, which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence.
Building out the data and model layer
“We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen, co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord, a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month.
The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said.
Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen.
We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted.
More winners
Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others.
Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year.
“There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen.

Ember: Home Batteries Could Cut India’s Solar Exports By 90%
Ember recommends extending PM Surya Ghar subsidies to batteries to boost rooftop solar-plus-storage systems adoption 
Key Takeaways
- Ember recommends extending subsidies to home batteries under India’s PM Surya Ghar scheme
- A 5 kWh battery could cut daytime solar exports by 85%-90%, but extend the payback period from 3.3 years to around 9 years, without subsidies
- A 50% battery subsidy could reduce payback to 6.3 years, while adding up to 25 GWh of distributed storage capacity
Home batteries could cut daytime rooftop solar exports to the grid in India by 85% to 90%, according to Ember, but high upfront costs limit their scope. Analysts recommend that the government subsidize batteries to accelerate their adoption.
In its analysis, Ember modeled a 3 kW rooftop solar system for a household using 350 units per month. This costs INR 87,000 after the INR 78,000 PM Surya Ghar subsidy and pays back in 3.3 years.
Analysts believe adding a 5 kWh battery system could cut daytime exports by 85% to 90%, shifting about 1,600 to 1,800 units a year to the evening. It will, however, be an expensive proposition, stretching the payback period to nine years.
At the same time, analysts believe that because India’s net metering system lets households use daytime solar exports to offset evening power use, households have no financial incentive to install batteries. Under the arrangement, discoms must compensate households for solar power exported during the day, even though they may have to buy electricity at a much higher price to meet demand in the evening.
Ember analysts recommend offering subsidies, preferably under the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (PMSGMBY), to cover battery costs. A 50% subsidy, for instance, could bring down the payback period for a solar-plus-battery system to 6.3 years. PM Surya Ghar targets 10 million solar rooftops and 30 GW installed PV capacity (see India Eyeing 30 GW Rooftop Solar Capacity With New Scheme).
“Subsidising hybrid systems for even half of the current scheme’s 10 million target would create 15–25 GWh of distributed storage,” says Ember.
Supporting hybrid systems for 5 million households could create 15–25 GWh of distributed storage capacity, requiring around INR 280 billion in financial support. State governments could also offer additional battery subsidies to reduce upfront costs for households.
Batteries installed now would also prepare households for future reforms, according to analysts. They identify two possible policy scenarios: limiting banked solar exports and restricting their use during peak hours. With a 40% cap on banked solar exports, the estimated payback period for a subsidized hybrid rooftop solar system falls to 6.5 years, and 5.7 years under peak-hour (6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.) restrictions and a 20% surcharge.
Ruchita Shah, Ember Energy Analyst Asia, believes India should integrate battery storage with rooftop solar installations under PM Surya Ghar to manage future grid challenges. Drawing on Australia and the US, she notes that solar power’s value depends not only on how much electricity it generates, but also on when it is used.
Titled Plugging storage into India’s rooftop solar revolution, the Ember analysis is available for free download on its website.
In an earlier report, Ember said solar paired with battery storage could supply most of India’s electricity at competitive costs, supplying about 90% of the country’s electricity at about INR 5.06/kWh (see Ember: Solar, Storage Could Meet 90% Of India’s Power Demand).

Gujarat and Rajasthan have declared drought in a total of 18 districts following deficient monsoon rainfall, with Gujarat announcing a relief package for farmers whose crops have failed.
The Rajasthan government declared drought in 14 of its 41 districts, while Gujarat identified four districts — Devbhumi Dwarka, Porbandar, Jamnagar and Kutch — as drought-hit.
In Rajasthan, the affected districts include Churu, Jaisalmer, Jalore, Pali, Jodhpur, Bikaner, Barmer and Balotra, among others.
According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Rajasthan received 340.2mm of rainfall during the monsoon season, from June 1 to September 30, 2026, against a normal of 435.6mm. This represents a rainfall deficit of 22 per cent.
On October 26, Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel announced relief measures for farmers in the four affected districts.
“This season, the state overall received around 89 per cent rainfall. However, Devbhumi Dwarka, Porbandar, Kutch, and Jamnagar districts witnessed lower rainfall,” Patel said in Gandhinagar.
He said the government had decided to support farmers affected by the rainfall deficit.
According to Patel, the decision was taken in accordance with the Centre's Drought Manual Guidelines, 2016. Farmers in the four districts will receive compensation for crop losses under the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) norms.
The state government will provide financial assistance of Rs 8,500 per hectare, capped at two hectares per farmer.
It has also begun supplying fodder at a subsidised rate of Rs 2 per kilogramme.
Other measures announced include 150 days of employment under the Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar & Ajeevika Mission (Gramin), or VB-G RAM G, in affected districts from November 1.
The government will also provide Rs 80 per animal to cattle shelters for livestock upkeep.
Gujarat and Rajasthan join Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh, which had previously declared drought in parts of their states.

Two Israeli TV networks have now updated their exit polls and are predicting that Netanyahu’s bloc will be tied with Eisenkot’s opposition grouping.
Kan 11 and Channel 13, two of the country’s leading broadcasters, have revised their exit poll to put the Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs tied on 51 seats each. Channel 12, the other main broadcaster, has Netanyahu’s bloc on 50 seats and the opposition on 52 seats – narrowing their projections from earlier in the night.
A candidate needs 61 parliamentary seats to form a majority coalition government.
Exit polls released earlier on Tuesday evening had Eisenkot winning most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin. Israeli exit polls are often revised after publication and are notoriously imprecise, with the final count often swinging by several seats.
Earlier in the evening, Avigdor Lieberman, head of the Yisrael Beitenu party, warned supporters that the final results could still change after hundreds of thousands of absentee ballots cast by on-duty soldiers are counted in the coming days.
Nadav Eyal, a columnist in the daily newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, has said that the revised exit polls show its going to be a long night for election watchers.
Historically, Israeli exit polls have tended to underestimate Likud, but shifts between blocs are usually limited to 2–3 seats at most.
Meanwhile a minister from Netanyahu’s party has told the Associated Press he’s cautiously optimistic about the results.
Amichai Chikli, minister for diaspora affairs for Israel’s government, said it was too early to celebrate the initial poll results but that the party was optimistic and had to be patient.
“One thing we know for sure, those who said Netanyahu is over, the Likud is over, celebrated too early,” he said.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats, has hinted that the opposition bloc could include Palestinian parties in its coalition, according to Haaretz.
Golan, who represents the last remnants of Israel’s once dominant Labour party, has policies on Gaza and a two state solution, that track towards a more centrist position in Israeli terms.
Speaking to supporters, Golan said “every Knesset member elected in the democratic, legal process is a legitimate part of our political system. If there is a democratic majority to replace the government of destruction – we must actualise it.”

Analysis: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival.
In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that.
The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, currently projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored.
Eisenkot will argue that he commands the bigger overall bloc and has the better chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List).
They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben Gvir in this election”.

Negotiations with the Joint List, with 10 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinians Israeli citizens, who are currently exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks.

Ben-Gvir’s extremist, ultranationalist party was expected to better their result of six seats from the 2022 elections.

Counting is under way in what many Israelis have described as the most consequential election in their country’s history, and we expect the first round of official results to come through around 1am local time on Wednesday. It comes after record turnout had reached 77.7% as of 10pm on Tuesday, with the historic election marked by a record participation by Israeli Arab voters.
Exit polls suggest that a majority of Israelis have voted against Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition, issuing a sharp rebuke to the prime minister, whose political and personal future hangs in the balance. His coalition bloc is projected to win only 50 seats, a loss of 14 since the 2022 election. And while his Likud party is narrowly projected to come out as the largest party by one or two seats, this still represents a loss for the party of 25% of its seats compared to the last election in 2022. Netanyahu is thus likely to fall short of the support required to form a new coalition. In an election widely seen as a referedum on his leadership since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks, Netanyahu has certainly lost his mandate.
His main challenger Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc, meanwhile, is projected to win 52 or 53 seats, and therefore also remains short of the 61 Knesset seats needed to make a majority. There is therefore no outright winner and no simple path to power for either Eisenkot or Netanyahu, and this result is likely to set off weeks of jockeying over who can form a coalition government before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is called.

beyond-your-beat-c82d135fe0.headline: In a first since 2023, Delhi invites Pakistan Minister for inaugural SCO Civilisational Dialogue in November
beyond-your-beat-c82d135fe0.fulltext:
India will hold the first “Civilisational Dialogue Forum” of the 10-nation Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) grouping, that includes Pakistan, from November 20-22 in Delhi, sources confirmed to The Hindu.
The dialogue, which will be organised by the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of External Affairs, was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO leaders’ Summit in Tianjin last year and adopted by the SCO Council. According to the sources, the government has invited Pakistan’s Minister for National Heritage and Culture Aurungzeb Khan Khichi, for the event. Culture Ministers from the 10 member states, including China, Russia, Iran, Belarus and Central Asian states, 15 Dialogue partners and observer countries have been invited.
Also Read | Days after India-Pakistan sparring at UN, senior Indian official visits Islamabad for SCO planning meet
The event, which will be inaugurated by Mr. Modi, will be held at Delhi’s iconic Purana Quila (Old Fort), a 16th Century fort built by Emperor Humayun. The fort is also the site of many excavations showcasing India’s ancient past spanning nearly 3,000 years, from the Pre-Mauryan, Mauryan, Sunga, Kushana, Gupta, Post-Gupta period to medieval-era Rajput, Sultanate and Mughal periods, officials said, explaining its importance.
According to diplomatic sources, Pakistan has not so far confirmed who will lead its delegation to the dialogue forum. If Mr. Khichi attends, this will be the first time India will host a Minister from Pakistan since the 2023 SCO Foreign Ministers meeting, when the then Pakistan FM Bilawal Bhutto had travelled to Goa, and the first since the four-day conflict between India and Pakistan in May 2025.
While the Modi government has refused to take part in meetings of South Asia Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) in Islamabad due to differences with Pakistan since 2016, it has joined SCO meetings there in the past, including SCO-Regional Anti-Terror Structure (RATS). In September, India sent SCO National Coordinator Alok Dimri to Islamabad to attend the first coordination meeting for Pakistan’s SCO Presidency and events leading up to the leader’s Summit in Pakistan, scheduled for August 2027. In November 2024, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar had represented India at the SCO Heads of Government (HoG) Meeting, and all eyes will be in who will represent India at the SCO Heads of State Summit next year.
Also Read | At SCO meet, Rajnath calls for dismantling the entire ecosystem of terrorism
“India deals with SCO as an entity, as an important organisation,” MEA Secretary (West) Sibi George said in response to a question from The Hindu at a briefing on August 27 about whether PM Modi would travel to Pakistan for the summit. “As far as our engagement with individual countries is concerned, a decision will be taken by the appropriate authority at the appropriate time and our appropriate level of participation will be decided accordingly”, he added.
As a part of the Civilisational Dialogue Forum, each participating State has been invited to nominate a delegation comprising the Minister responsible for Culture and up to four government representatives, including senior officials, subject-matter experts, scholars, cultural heritage professionals or representatives of relevant cultural institutions. The Forum aims to promote awareness and appreciation of the shared civilisational heritage of SCO countries, organisers said and will feature four thematic sessions: Monastic Trails, involving Religion and Philosophical Traditions; Art and Architecture; Language, Literature, Script and Manuscript Traditions; and Cultural Expressions and Living Traditions within all the countries in the grouping.

world-91b856760d.headline: What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
world-91b856760d.fulltext:
When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

Vadra, the son of the Congress leader, Priyanka Gandhi, defended his work and also refused a request to remove images featuring the national flag. In a press statement, the venue said certain photos were “inconsistent” with its policy.
Fashion | Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee, celebrated for his maximalist aesthetic, hosted a Diwali party at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. In September, he unveiled a high-jewellery collection inspired by the Byzantine, in collaboration with the museum.

A recommendation from someone with great taste
Film-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annual Dharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:
“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
7,633
That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.
Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

india-deep-tech-6003c17a0f.fulltext:
Physical Intelligence, a startup that develops AI software to power robots, is in talks to raise money at a valuation of about $20 billion, according to Bloomberg.
The company is discussing a round of at least $1 billion, with existing backers Avenir and Lux Capital in talks to lead it, according to Bloomberg. Physical Intelligence, Avenir and Lux Capital did not respond to Bloomberg's requests for comment.
Physical Intelligence secured funding that valued it at $11.5 billion this year, according to Bloomberg. The company has no revenue, according to Bloomberg.
Other backers include CapitalG, Alphabet $GOOGL +1.19%'s independent growth fund, Amazon $AMZN +1.61%.com founder Jeff Bezos and Thrive Capital, according to Bloomberg. Onetime Google DeepMind researchers teamed up with academics at Stanford University and the University of California, Berkeley, to start the company in 2024.
This month, Physical Intelligence began letting outside developers use and tailor its newest robotics models, according to Bloomberg. The option is in beta and has increased investor interest in the fundraising, according to Bloomberg.
"Real-world robotic applications are not easy," the startup wrote when it announced the launch, according to Bloomberg. "Tackling robotic construction, robotic surgery, or warehouse automation each requires an entire company."
Physical Intelligence says its AI works across many kinds of hardware from other makers and can carry out numerous different robot motions, according to Bloomberg.
OpenAI and Elon Musk's Tesla $TSLA +4.04% are among a growing number of startups and bigger companies that compete with the company, according to Bloomberg. Skild AI, another startup centered on teaching robots to learn, reached a $14 billion valuation when it raised funds in January. Skild AI announced in September that its annual recurring revenue had passed $100 million, according to Bloomberg.

india-deep-tech-311c33af79.headline: Crunchbase Data Shows Q3 Robotics Startup Funding Jumps 185% As US And China Lead Physical AI Push
india-deep-tech-311c33af79.fulltext:
Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with the bulk of investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1.
It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year.
China and the US lead
The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested.
The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics, a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics, which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round.
In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI, which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain.
Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics, which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence.
Building out the data and model layer
“We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen, co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord, a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month.
The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said.
Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen.
We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted.
More winners
Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others.
Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year.
“There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen.

ai-a9a2cf8c96.headline: Who’s really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO?
ai-a9a2cf8c96.fulltext:
Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term. As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets.
Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley. But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board.
First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety. That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors.
Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi. There is one vacancy on the board.
Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity. The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors. The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs. There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now. The existing members will themselves choose who fills it.
Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors. If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock.
Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT. When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote.
Here’s what all that looks like:
The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict. We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was not being candid with them. Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place. Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power.
At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries.
The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain. At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board.
If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control.
